anti_overlap: fd-payments-schema-governance covers enum closedness and version governance of the schema, not tier-routing/scheduling semantics
fd-labmed-chain-of-custody covers provenance lineage and destruction-gating, not tier-capability enforcement
fd-aviation-mro-compliance-record covers regulatory certification gating of stage sign-off, which is a different kind of gate than capability-based tier routing
distance_rationale: Post-production pipelines are a parallel discipline: they route the same source material through a staged sequence of tools of increasing cost/capability (on-set proxy -> editorial -> color/VFX -> DCP delivery) built by different teams in different software stacks, but the domain is creative-media delivery rather than privacy compliance and the constraint is throughput/deadline rather than legal risk.
expected_isomorphisms: Proxy-first workflows (cut low-res proxies now, conform to camera-original later), stage-declared minimum capability requirements (an online color grade cannot run on a laptop that can run an offline edit), and content-addressed media identity via EDLs/reels map directly onto tiered stage routing (device_realtime -> cloud_burst), per-stage minimum_tier declarations, and content-addressed session artifacts.
focus: Staged tier-routing correctness and multi-runtime handoff mechanics for a pipeline that must degrade gracefully under resource constraints.
name: fd-postproduction-pipeline-staging
persona: Apply the perspective of a post-production pipeline supervisor (DIT/pipeline TD managing dailies-to-delivery workflow across edit, VFX, and color facilities) — they care about whether every stage's minimum-capability requirement is declared and enforced before work is routed to it; they measure the pipeline by whether a shot silently routed to the wrong facility/tier is caught before the wrong output ships; they flag any point where the contract doesn't make it impossible to send finishing-tier work through a proxy-tier stage by accident.
review_areas: Whether minimum_tier is enforced as a hard contract precondition (the scheduler cannot route below-tier work) versus an advisory field a stage implementation could ignore, mirroring the difference between a hard capability gate and a suggested workflow step in post pipelines

Whether the stage interface models graceful degradation/partial-completion (a stage that starts on one tier and must hand off mid-work to another) at all, given the brief's later frame-selective-capture and thermal-degradation requirements will need this

Whether the no-op stage skeleton in each language actually proves the *routing* contract (declares real inputs/outputs/tier/privacy_class metadata) or merely proves the languages can compile a stub, leaving tier-routing semantics unvalidated until M1

Whether the contract distinguishes a stage's declared minimum_tier from the artifact's required destination trust level, since post-pipelines learned the hard way that 'which facility can do this work' and 'where is this asset allowed to live' are separate axes that get conflated and cause leaks

Whether session manifests can express a session whose stages ran across multiple tiers/machines over time (device now, node later) without ambiguity about ordering or partial state, the way an EDL must survive assembly across multiple facilities

Whether the fixtures directory's conformance vectors include a case of a stage declaration requesting a tier/privacy_class combination that should be rejected by the scheduler, not just schema-invalid documents

severity_examples.condition: Without this as an enforced contract property from M0, tier-routing bugs (e.g., garment segmentation attempted on-device under thermal throttle) become a runtime behavior bug discovered at M1-M4 instead of a contract violation caught by shared conformance tests.
severity_examples.scenario: The pipeline contract's minimum_tier field is documented as informational metadata with no accompanying schema rule or conformance vector proving a scheduler must refuse to run a stage below its declared tier.

severity_examples.condition: The brief's own storage-ceiling policy (raw reclaimed only once every routed stage confirms) requires exactly this kind of partial/pending state; if M0's schema can't express 'stage X pending on tier Y' cleanly, M1's storage/reclaim logic will bolt on an ad hoc side-channel instead of using the contract.
severity_examples.scenario: The stage interface and manifest schema have no representation for a stage that is declared but has not yet run, or has run on one tier and awaits confirmation from a stage on another tier.

severity_examples.condition: This is the same gap post-pipelines hit when an EDL is technically well-formed XML but references a reel that violates delivery-spec rules — schema validity alone doesn't catch domain-rule violations, and the brainstorm's own flow-rule table needs its own semantic fixture class.
severity_examples.scenario: Fixture conformance vectors validate schema shape only (well-formed vs malformed JSON against the schema) with no vector representing a semantically-invalid but schema-valid combination, e.g., a stage claiming minimum_tier: device_realtime while privacy_class: raw_quarantined targets a destination the flow rules forbid.

source_domain: Film/broadcast post-production pipeline engineering (dailies -> editorial -> VFX/color -> delivery, multi-vendor tool handoffs)
success_hints: Confirms minimum_tier is a schema-enforceable precondition with at least one conformance vector proving rejection of an under-tier routing attempt, not just documented as descriptive metadata
Confirms the manifest/stage-interface schema can express a stage in a pending/partial state across a tier handoff, anticipating the storage-ceiling and dead-letter requirements coming in M1-M3
Confirms fixtures include semantically-invalid-but-schema-valid vectors (rule violations), not only structurally-invalid JSON
Distinguishes stage minimum_tier (capability requirement) from privacy_class destination rules (trust requirement) as two separate, non-conflated schema axes
task_context: Reviewing an M0 brainstorm for a JSON-Schema-first, dual-language (Swift/Python) pipeline contract defining a stage interface with (inputs, outputs, minimum_tier, privacy_class), a tiered scheduler contract, and content-addressed session manifests, ahead of later milestones that add real tiered/thermal/storage-driven routing behavior.
